title: Workflows or agents: who owns the control flow?

items.stem: Two systems both call a language model and both call tools. What most clearly separates an agent from a workflow?

options.text: The agent calls more than one tool per request
The model, not the code, picks each next step
The agent runs on a larger and stronger model
The agent keeps memory between separate sessions

items.stem: A booking helper always runs these steps in this order: extract the date from the student's message, check the calendar, book the slot, send a confirmation. A model call writes the confirmation text, but the program's code decides which step comes next. What is this system?

options.text: An agent, because it calls tools to take actions
An agent, because a model writes some of its text
A workflow, because its order of steps is not fixed
A workflow, because the code, not the model, sets the order

items.stem: Which situation is the best reason to build one part of an assistant as a fixed workflow instead of an agent?

options.text: The steps are the same every time, and cost per request must stay low
Requests vary so much that nobody can list the steps in advance
The system must handle questions that nobody on the team predicted
The system should keep trying different tools until one of them works

items.stem: A student asks the assistant: "Which laser cutter is free on Friday, and do I need a safety course to use it?" If the assistant is built as an agent, who decides which tools get called and in what order? Answer in a few words.

A team splits its makerspace assistant in two parts. Part 1 books a slot after the student confirms; its steps are always the same. Part 2 helps a student work out why a machine is misbehaving; which lookups it needs depends on what each earlier result shows. Which design is best?

options.text: Both parts as agents, since agents always give better results
Both parts as workflows, since workflows can never go wrong
Part 1 as a fixed workflow and Part 2 as an agent
Part 1 as an agent and Part 2 as a fixed workflow

items.stem: A fixed workflow makes exactly 3 model calls per request. An agent doing the same job averages 7 model calls per request, because it loops. Assume every model call costs $0.02. Over 500 requests, how much more does the agent cost than the workflow, in dollars?
